newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HKMA says cannot rule out tight mortgage criteria.
newsitem.headline: HKMA says cannot rule out tight mortgage criteria.

text.p: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said on Thursday it cannot rule out the possibility of asking banks to tighten mortgage lending criteria in the wake of a reheating in the local property market.
"We haven't yet taken a view that we need to ask the banks in general to tighten the lending critria," David Carse, deputy chief executive of the HKMA, told reporters.

"I can't rule out the possibility that we might ask the banks to tighten the criteria at some time in the future if it appears that the amount of speculation in the market is increasing or we continue to have a very rapid rise of prices."
Hong Kong residential property prices rose an average of 24 percent last year. The government has warned there were signs of speculation in the luxury market, where prices surged about 35 percent.
Carse said it would not be the function of the HKMA, Hong Kong's de facto central bank, to try to regulate the property market.
But the appearance of an asset price bubble could add an element of risk, and in this situation the HKMA could ask the banks to tighten criteria, he said.
"Not disputing that mortgage lending is a very safe form of lending under normal circumstances, we think it's prudent that the banks don't have too many eggs in one basket," he said.

The HKMA issued a warning to banks in December, after it announced an increase in outstanding mortgages in November, to draw their attention to increasing speculation in the property market, particularly at the more expensive end, Carse said.

Carse said the establishment of a mortgage corporation under the HKMA, which he expected to be up and running in the second half of the year, would be a fundamental solution to the mismatch of banks' long-term mortgage lending and shorter-term borrowing.
"That would enable the banks to adjust their portfolios so that they don't become over-concentrated and that also adds liquidity to their portfolios," he said.
